deep.reconstruction:
The only original writing on folio 8v is the symbol in the upper left corner: P(α over α', β over β', γ over γ', x). Everything else visible is ink showing through from the other side of the leaf, in mirror image. That text matches the previous page's transcription line for line: 'Es fragt sich also, wo sie unendlich werden…', the excluded neighbourhoods of 0, ∞ and 1, 'Die Function p = −d log(y1 dy2/dlog x − y2 dy1/dlog x)/dlog x', '∫ p d log x … = 2πi Σλ', and so on. A faint pencil layer, also mirrored, is likewise from the reverse. Neither belongs to this page. A strip of the following sheet, matching the next-page transcription ('Sind die … Glieder…'), is visible at the right edge.

Meaning of the symbol in modern terms: it is Riemann's P-symbol. It denotes the class of multivalued functions whose branches satisfy a second-order Fuchsian equation with exactly three regular singular points. The column α/α' gives the pair of local exponents at the first singular point, β/β' at the second, and γ/γ' at the third. The order 0, ∞, 1 is inferred from the 1857 paper and the surrounding pages, not written here.

In the 1857 paper the full symbol is P{a b c; α β γ; α' β' γ'; x}, with the singular points written in the top row. This sheet suppresses that row, so the points are fixed as 0, ∞, 1. The surrounding sheets (8r, 9r) derive the constraint on the exponents via the Wronskian. They show that y' dy''/dlog x − y'' dy'/dlog x behaves like x^{α+β} near 0, like (1−x)^{α'+β'} near 1 and like (1/x)^{α''+β''} near ∞. Since the Wronskian is single-valued and has no other zeros or poles, it equals a constant times these powers. From this the coefficients p and q follow, and with them the condition that the six exponents sum to 1. The corner symbol on 8v is presumably a heading or label for that work. No derivation is carried out on this page itself.

results.what: Notation P(α α', β β', γ γ', x) for functions with three branch points (here implicitly 0, ∞, 1) and exponent pairs at each point
results.modern_name: Riemann P-symbol (Riemann scheme) for the Riemann–Papperitz / hypergeometric equation
results.usually_credited_to: Bernhard Riemann, 1857 ('Beiträge zur Theorie der durch die Gauss'sche Reihe F(α,β,γ,x) darstellbaren Functionen')

deep.surprise_reason: The page contains only Riemann's own P-symbol, which he published in 1857. The rest is mirror-image show-through from the other side of the leaf (the previous page), so there is no new mathematical content.

checkable.asserts: For Gauss's hypergeometric equation the exponents (0, 1−c at x=0; 0, c−a−b at x=1; a, b at ∞) sum to 1. This is the Riemann/Fuchs relation α+α'+β+β'+γ+γ'=1 for a P-function.

checkable.sympy: x,a,b,c=symbols('x a b c'); W=x**(-c)*(1-x)**(c-a-b-1); p=(c-(a+b+1)*x)/(x*(1-x)); simplify(diff(W,x)+p*W)==0
checkable.asserts: The Wronskian of the hypergeometric equation y''+p y'+q y=0 is W = C x^{-c}(1−x)^{c−a−b−1}. This is consistent with the Wronskian argument on the adjacent sheets, where the exponents of the Wronskian at each singular point are the sums of the local exponents shifted by the order of differentiation.

transcription_corrections: The machine transcription is right to record only the P-symbol. Almost all the dark writing in the image is mirror-image bleed-through of the recto (the previous page's text) and must not be read as content of folio 8v.
The symbol reads P(α/α', β/β', γ/γ', x): each pair is stacked vertically with the unprimed exponent above, matching the transcription's matrix layout. No singular points are written in a top row.
